tone_statements.citation: Li, Jinfang and Luo, Yongxian (2010). The Buyang language of South China: Grammatical notes, glossary, texts and translations. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University. 231 pp.
tone_statements.quote: There are 7 tones in Paha Buyang, which is the most developed among the Geyang group. ... High level ⁵⁵ ti⁵⁵ ‘one’ (citation form) ... High rise ⁴⁵ ti⁴⁵ ‘one’ (used with classifiers) ... Mid level ³³ ti³³ ‘pair’ ... Mid fall ³²² ti³²² ‘empty’ ... Low fall ³¹ ti³¹ ‘wash’ ... Mid rise ²⁴ ti²⁴ ‘to whittle’ ... Low level ¹¹ ti¹¹ ‘small bowl’ ... The mid falling tone ³²² starts with fall, and then a long level. Low level tone ¹¹ is slightly lower. ... A number of prefixes are pronounced with the neutral tone, labelled as ⁰.
tone_statements.summary: 7 tones with Chao values, shown by 7-way minimal sets on ti and taŋ; neutral-tone (0) prefixes; complex tone sandhi left unanalysed; 55~33 and 45~24 hard to tell apart in connected speech.

tone_statements.summary: Identification of the work's 'Paha' (Chinese characters dropped in extraction) with catalog 'Baha Buyang' rests on the name only. Paha forms carry pitch numerals (pa322 'four', pe45 'dear', maan31 'new', tu322 'three', du322 'to do', pa33 nau33 k33 pi45 aai45 a31 'nobody knows'), so tonal. Second-hand (materials from Li).

tone_statements.citation: Li, Jinfang and Luo, Yongxian (2006). Notes on Paha Buyang. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 29. pp. 1-40.
tone_statements.quote: There are 7 tones in Paha Buyang, which is the most developed among the Kra (Kadai) group. [...] High level 55 / High rising 45 / Mid level 33 / Mid falling 322 / Low falling 31 / Mid rising 24 / Low level 11 [tone table, p. 8]. The mid falling tone 322 starts with a fall, then levels out. The low level tone 11 is slightly lower. In connected speech and in bisyllabic or polysyllabic words, high level and mid level tones are not easily distinguishable. The same is true of high rise and mid rise tones. There are no voice quality differences among the tones. [p. 9] A number of prefixes are pronounced with the neutral tone, labelled as 0 [...] Other prefixes may carry either a phonemic tone or the neutral tone. [p. 9] Tone sandhi is a common phenomenon of Paha Buyang, exhibiting very complex features. We haven not yet been able to come up with any generalisations on the mechanisms of tone sandhi in Paha Buyang. [p. 9]
tone_statements.locator: Section 2.1.3 Tones, printed pp. 8-9; conclusion p. 32: 'Like Kam-Tai, Paha has a rich tonal system'
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Seven contrastive lexical tones on monosyllables (55, 45, 33, 322, 31, 24, 11, Chao letters) plus a neutral tone (0) on some prefixes; no voice-quality (register) differences among tones. Distributional restrictions: checked syllables take mostly 55, 33, 31, 11 and rarely 45, 24, 322 except with long vowels; aspirated initials occur mostly with 33 and 45; voiced vs voiced-aspirated stop contrast i

sources.citation: Li Jinfang & Luo Yongxian. 2010. The Buyang language of South China: grammatical notes, glossary, texts and translations. Pacific Linguistics 607. Canberra: ANU. xii+231 pp. (open access, CC BY-SA, hdl 1885/146755)
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent anywhere (searched full text). Ch. 2 (pp. 9-14): 7 lexical tones; 'A number of prefixes are pronounced with the neutral tone, labelled as 0.. compare these structurally to the sesquisyllabic wordshape'; other prefixes alternate full tone ~ neutral tone; complex unanalysed tone sandhi; first syllables of compounds may lose final nasals/stops.
